title: What is a caravan in law
paras: So — what is a caravan in law? Everything starts in the same place: section twenty-nine, subsection one, of the Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960. A caravan is a structure designed or adapted for human habitation which is capable of being moved from one place to another — whether by towing, or by transport on a motor vehicle or trailer. Three things fall out of that. First, the structure has to be designed or adapted for living in. What it looks like doesn't matter — house, hut, whatever — which is exactly why containers, converted horseboxes and modular cabins get tested on the definition and not on appearance. Second, it has to be capable of being moved. And third, it is expressly not a building. Parliament wanted caravans treated as chattels, unless the way they're installed later tips over into building operations.

"Capable of being moved" is about physical capability, not convenience. The courts — Bunn is the one to remember — took it to mean movable without structural damage, by normal methods: towing, lifting, craning, or a low-loader. It doesn't need wheels. It doesn't need to be moved regularly. And whether you could lawfully move it on the highway is beside the point — an oversize load needing a special escort still passes. What actually defeats mobility is physical: brick skirts tied into the structure, anchoring bolts or plates fixed through the chassis, deep concrete bases, or porches and steps built in so that taking it away means demolition.

Inspectors now frame the whole thing as three tests — size, construction and assembly, and mobility — and every limb has to be met. Fail any one and the structure simply isn't a caravan. It's presumptively a building, its siting becomes operational development, planning permission is required unless a permitted development right applies, fees go floor-area based, and enforcement gets a great deal easier for the authority. Pass all three and you've got a caravan — usually a chattel — and its siting isn't development unless the use of the land has materially changed.

Now, two regulatory regimes overlap here, and you have to keep them apart. The Caravan Sites Acts define what a caravan is and run the site-licensing system — safety, spacing, amenity standards. They don't grant planning permission. The Town and Country Planning Act 1990 — the T-C-P-A — regulates development and material changes of use, and it couldn't care less what the licence says. A structure can be a caravan for licensing purposes and still involve development in planning terms. So an enforcement notice citing licensing breaches has already made a legal misstep. The Acts describe a structure; the T-C-P-A regulates what you do with it.

title: Twin units and the size limits
paras: Now, twin units and the size limits. Section thirteen of the Caravan Sites Act 1968 stretches the definition to cover twin-unit caravans — Parliament's answer to homes too big to move in one piece. Its tests sit on top of the 1960 Act, and there are three. First, no more than two sections, built separately and designed to be assembled on site. Second, joined only by bolts, clamps or other devices — the final act of assembly has to be a simple mechanical joining operation, not construction work like building a house. And third, physically capable of being moved once assembled — even if moving it on the highway would need a special escort.

The dimensional limits were last amended in 2006: twenty metres in length, excluding the drawbar; six point eight metres in width; and three point zero five metres internal height of the living accommodation. Go over any one of those and the structure isn't a caravan. And the consequence lands immediately — it becomes a building for planning purposes unless you can show otherwise. Even a small breach is fatal: an internal height of three point zero seven metres fails. Worth saying too — the roof void doesn't count as living accommodation for the height measurement, and that point has decided appeals.

The construction and assembly test won't tolerate structural welding on site, cutting and reframing walls or floors, construction by traditional building methods, brickwork skirting forming permanent support, or deep concrete foundations. Inspectors read it strictly and literally — if the way it's joined looks like building works rather than a mechanical connection, it fails. And the classic failures? The twin-unit delivered in halves that then needs internal walls put up, structural timber to join the roof sections, or concrete pads poured specially for it. Structures like that get found to be operational development time and again.

Single units throw up different issues from twins. Delivered complete, they usually turn on mobility after installation — a single unit often fails because the installation has become too permanent. Twin units generate most of the appeals, because they hang on section thirteen, and it's their installation where authorities allege building operations. Here's the thing about the supports: non-permanent systems — jack legs, proprietary pad systems — aren't foundations, and they aren't a structural third section either. And the line between those and poured bases is often the whole case.

title: When a caravan is development
paras: So when is a caravan development? Section fifty-five of the T-C-P-A 1990 defines development in two limbs — operational development, and material change of use — and those give you the two questions every caravan case has to answer. Is the caravan a building, or installed by building operations? And does its use amount to a material change of use of the land? A structure can satisfy every limb of the statutory caravan definition and still be development by either route.

The Measor case, back in 1998, settled that a structure meeting the caravan definition usually won't be a building, because it lacks the necessary permanence — caravans rest on temporary supports and you can move them without demolition. But Measor didn't say a caravan can never be a building. The Carter and Byrne line asks whether the installation itself amounts to building operations: deep or continuous foundations, anchors fixed into the ground, structural brick skirting, permanent buried services incompatible with removal, structurally integrated porches, decking or extensions — or a structure you can only remove by dismantling it beyond the simple separation section thirteen permits. And the permanence analysis leans on Barvis and Elitestone: size, permanence, physical attachment.

Even an undisputed caravan can be development through its use. A new planning unit forms once the caravan gets its own curtilage, parking or access and runs as an independent household. Residential use starting on agricultural land is almost always a material change. And intensification — more units, or year-round occupation of a seasonal site — can shift the character of the use even where each unit, on its own, is perfectly lawful.

The recent appeal record shows an Inspectorate that's disciplined and statute-led. Take a twin-unit in a garden — bolted together, on jacks, reversible services, integrated ancillary occupation — held to be a caravan whose siting wasn't development. The fact that nobody ever intended to move it made no difference. Then a visually similar garden "annexe", built in situ on poured concrete pads, with an integral sub-frame and fixed steps: that one failed on mobility and was a building put up by operational development — the neighbours' construction photographs beating the applicant's generic factory images. And an enforcement notice alleging "residential use of the land" was varied, because the right breach was the material change of use to the stationing of a caravan for residential purposes. Same subject matter, opposite outcomes — decided entirely on the installation facts and precise analysis.

title: Ancillary caravan or independent dwelling
paras: Ancillary caravan, or independent dwelling? Start with curtilage. Curtilage is a factual assessment, not a legal fiction: the land immediately surrounding a dwelling, used for purposes intimately associated with its enjoyment. You judge it on physical layout, functional association, patterns of use and enclosure — and Land Registry boundaries don't come into it. A caravan within the curtilage may sit inside the same planning unit. One stationed in the paddock or field beyond it almost always creates a new use of land once it's occupied residentially. And be precise with the terms. Incidental use — a home office, hobby space, the occasional guest sleeping over — and ancillary use — living accommodation that supports and forms part of the main dwelling's residential function — are distinct, and both are different again from independence.

The planning unit test comes from Burdle: the unit of occupation, and the purpose for which the land is used. No new unit forms where occupation is part of the same household, domestic life is integrated, nothing's fenced off or treated separately, and there's no independent access or servicing. A separate unit — and with it, development — forms where occupation goes autonomous: its own access, garden, parking, postal identity, separate metering, a domestic life of its own. And here's the sharpest single question you can ask: would the caravan still function as a home if the main dwelling were taken away?

The contrast is what decides most cases. On one side, the twin-unit on jacks, connected by flexible services, the garden left undivided, the elderly relative sharing meals and domestic life with the household. That's within curtilage, integrated — no new planning unit, no development. On the other, the "garden lodge" with its own fenced area, decking, separate facilities, post coming to the door, and an independent domestic life. Structurally it's still a caravan — but in land-use terms it's a new dwellinghouse needing permission. Facilities don't decide independence; patterns of occupation do. And inspectors say so, consistently.

Temporary siting during a self-build is the special case that keeps coming back. The touring caravan is almost certainly lawful as a structure. The real question is whether occupation is genuinely temporary and tied to the building operations, or whether it's drifted into a new residential use of the land. Minimal supports, moving it when construction requires, removal at completion — those point one way. Multi-year settled family occupation points the other. Staff accommodation on commercial, equestrian or agricultural land is the same analysis in a different setting — the stationing is a change of use of land that needs its own justification, however lawful the business itself.

title: The 28-day rule and PD routes
paras: Let's turn to the twenty-eight-day rule and the permitted development routes. Two first principles govern every P-D argument in a caravan case. Permitted development rights only apply to development under section fifty-five — so if the siting isn't development, because it's a caravan, an ancillary use, the same planning unit, then P-D is simply irrelevant. The siting is already lawful. And P-D doesn't override the site-licensing regime or the Caravan Acts analysis. It only comes into play where the siting is development and the applicant leans on the General Permitted Development Order — the G-P-D-O — to avoid express permission.

Part 4, Class B permits the use of land for any purpose for not more than twenty-eight days in total in any calendar year. That's aggregate, not consecutive — and it's a right over the use of the land, not the use of the caravan. It legitimately covers temporary events, seasonal activities and the occasional touring visitor. What it doesn't do is permit operational development. It doesn't create an entitlement to live in a caravan for twenty-eight days. And you can't stretch it into quasi-permanent residential occupation by rolling declarations, or by rotating units through the same pitch. Inspectors turn those claims down consistently.

Part 4, Class A permits buildings and moveable structures — and a caravan can be one — required temporarily in connection with, and for the duration of, operations being carried out on that or adjoining land. The caravan has to be genuinely required by the works: a site office, a welfare unit, security or supervision accommodation. And the right falls away the moment the works finish. A caravan used as the family home right through a two-year self-build generally won't qualify, because the use is residential rather than construction-related. Authorities should be asking for the building contract, the programme, the purpose of the caravan, and how long it's meant to be there.

For caravans specifically, the sharper route is Part 5, not Part 4. Part 5, Class A grants permitted development for the use of land as a caravan site in the licence-exempt circumstances set out in Schedule 1 to the Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960. Paragraph 9 of that Schedule covers building and engineering sites. A caravan used for the accommodation of a person employed in connection with the operations on that or adjoining land needs neither a site licence nor express planning permission for the caravan-site use, for as long as the works run. Now, "employed" is undefined in the Act, and it's read fairly liberally as to who qualifies. But the accommodation has to be genuinely tied to the operations, and the right falls away — caravans removed — once the works cease. This is the caravan-specific mechanism, and it's a good deal more robust than stretching the Part 4 temporary-structure right to cover what is really residential occupation.

Part 6 agricultural rights don't authorise residential use of caravans, and they don't authorise static caravans as workers' dwellings. At most, in narrow circumstances, they allow a caravan as a temporary agricultural structure — not habitation. And no P-D route for temporary use authorises the operational development that so often comes with caravans: bases, foundations, engineered drainage, roads, hardstanding, structural decking — every bit of it needs its own justification. Nor does P-D ever permit a material change of use to a new dwellinghouse, or the formation of a separate planning unit.

title: LDCs, enforcement and the myths
paras: Finally — lawful development certificates, enforcement, and the myths. L-D-Cs matter more here than almost anywhere, because appearance is misleading, the decisive questions are questions of fact, and applicants want certainty against enforcement turning up years later. A section one-nine-one certificate — for existing lawfulness — is proved on the balance of probabilities: the exact physical characteristics, the installation method at the time of siting, the pattern and nature of the use — ancillary or independent — the duration where immunity is claimed, the planning unit, and the absence of building operations. It stands or falls on evidence, not on planning merits.

A section one-nine-two certificate — for a proposed development — is the forward-looking route: the proposed twin-unit within curtilage, the like-for-like replacement caravan, the self-build arrangement. Its strength is that method statements, engineering drawings and mobility evidence can all be weighed before anything is sited — and that buys certainty. The refusal errors you can predict? Rejecting it because the unit "might" be lived in independently. Treating bedrooms and bathrooms as inherently creating a dwelling. Misunderstanding the final act of assembly. And conflating site licensing with planning.

Enforcement has to target the correct breach — that's the golden rule, and getting it wrong is the single biggest cause of failure at appeal. Allege a material change of use of the land to the stationing of a caravan or mobile home for residential purposes where occupation is independent, where residential use has started on agricultural land, or where numbers have intensified the use. Allege the erection of a building, or building operations comprising the installation, where foundations, integral sub-frames, structural skirting or attached works have turned siting into construction. And where the caravan is lawful but the works beneath it aren't — hardstanding, bases, drainage — a split notice, requiring removal of the works while allowing the caravan, gets you there without overreach.

Route and fee follow the very same analysis. If the structure is a caravan and the use is ancillary, the L-D-C is the cleanest and cheapest route. It takes planning judgment and policy debate off the table, and it gives you enduring certainty. If any element is development — oversize, building-level assembly, foundations, an independent unit — the proposal needs a full application at the full fee. And misclassify it and you store up validation problems, and problems with the Community Infrastructure Levy — C-I-L. A genuine caravan attracts no C-I-L. But a structure that is in law a building, or a use that creates a dwellinghouse, engages it. So fee strategy is part of the legal assessment — not some late procedural step.
